subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Four Shape-Friends: First Read

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter by asking students what shapes they can name and what makes a good friend. This warm-up builds curiosity about why shapes might argue.

Teacher reads the story aloud from the textbook (pp.25–29), using different voices for Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle, and the star. Pauses at each shape's boast to ask: 'What is this shape saying about itself?'
Teacher leads a second reading with students following in their books. Students take turns reading one shape's speech each in a shared-reading format (pp.25–29).
Class discusses briefly: 'Why did the shapes need a star to help them?' Students share one-sentence responses orally before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The four shape-characters — Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle — each boast about a distinct property, so pause after each boast to let students visualise that shape. Watch for students who read 'rectangle' haltingly; model it syllable by syllable before moving on.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: What the Story Tells Us

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — items 1–5 (pp.29): factual questions and true/false on the shape-friends' argument.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly retells the story arc — four shapes boast, fail to agree, ask the star — without reading the book, to re-anchor the narrative. Students listen with books closed.

Let us think — items 1–4 (p.29): teacher poses each question orally, calls on volunteers, and guides the class to full-sentence answers — covering who the friends were, why they fought, who helped, and what lesson they learned.

Let us think — item 5 (p.29): teacher reads each true/false statement aloud; students show thumbs-up or thumbs-down, then explain their verdict in one sentence. Teacher confirms with a page reference.
Students write their answers to items 1–4 in their notebooks independently. Teacher circulates and gives brief oral feedback on sentence formation.

periods.teacher_notes: Common pitfall: students often answer item 2 with 'they were mean' rather than pointing to the specific boasting dispute; redirect them to what each shape claimed. For the true/false items, guide students to cite the story detail — for instance, the claim about the square's equal sides — rather than guessing.

periods.activity_title: Speaking About Friends and Shapes Around Us

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — items 6–7 (p.29): talk about a friend's help and shapes spotted around the room.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the conversation opener: 'My friend is Anu. When she helps me, I feel happy and we finish our work faster.' Students listen and notice the structure — name, then what friendship does.

Let us think — item 6 (p.29): in pairs, students take turns answering 'Who is your friend?' and 'What can you do when your friend helps you?' Teacher circulates and prompts with 'Can you say more about that?'

Let us think — item 7 (p.29): students look around the classroom and call out objects, saying the shape and where they see it — 'The door is a rectangle.' Teacher collects responses on the board and adds the shape name.
Three or four volunteers share a complete sentence about their friend and one about a shape they noticed. Class gives a thumbs-up if the sentence is clear and names a real shape or friendship act.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle boasting about their everyday uses, students are well-primed to spot those same shapes in the classroom. Encourage students to use the shapes' exact properties — 'it has four equal sides' — rather than just naming the shape.

periods.activity_title: Role-Play: Becoming Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle, and the Star

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.30): groups of five role-play each shape-character with actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher assigns roles — Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle, Star — and demonstrates one shape's boast with an action, e.g. arms forming a circle while saying 'I am round and beautiful with no sharp edges!'

Let us speak (p.30): groups of five rehearse the role-play, each student reading their character's lines and adding a matching gesture. Teacher moves group to group, prompting expression and clear enunciation.

Two groups perform for the class; the watching group listens and identifies which shape spoke first and what each shape boasted about. Brief class feedback focuses on audibility and character expression.
Class reflects together: 'Which character do you think gave the wisest answer and why?' Two or three students share a sentence before the unit ends.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the shapes' boasts as a class, students bring that knowledge into the performance; expect them to exaggerate the boasts with relish, which is exactly right. The star's lines carry the story's moral about friendship and collaboration — make sure the student playing the star speaks slowly and clearly so the message lands.
materials: Role-label cards (optional): Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle, Star

periods.activity_title: Articles 'A' and 'An': Exploring the Rule with Familiar Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.30): fill in the blank with 'a' before consonant-starting nouns.
Let us learn — B (p.31): fill in the blank with 'an' before vowel-starting nouns.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'a dog' and 'an eagle' on the board and reads them aloud. Students repeat, and the teacher asks: 'What sound does "dog" start with? What sound does "eagle" start with?' The consonant/vowel distinction is drawn out through student responses.

Let us learn — A (p.30): teacher reads each sentence aloud, students decide on 'a', write the answer, and explain why — 'dog starts with /d/, a consonant, so we use a.' All three sentences are completed together.
Let us learn — B (p.31): same process for 'an' with eagle, umbrella, and ice-cream. Teacher emphasises that 'an' comes before words that begin with a vowel sound.
Quick oral check: teacher says a noun from the story ('circle', 'eagle', 'apple', 'square') and students call out 'a' or 'an' and give a reason in one word — 'vowel' or 'consonant'.

periods.teacher_notes: The nouns in Part A — dog, cow, sparrow — are everyday words students already know, which keeps attention on the article rule rather than word meaning. Watch for 'an umbrella' pronounced as 'a umbrella'; model the linked pronunciation 'an_umbrella' slowly before students practise.

periods.activity_title: Choosing 'A' or 'An': Mixed Practice and Word Games

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — C (p.31): fill in 'a' or 'an' in mixed sentences with multiple blanks.

time_bands.activity: Teacher plays a quick word-sort game: calls out nouns ('apricot', 'building', 'orange', 'chikoo') one at a time; students hold up a card marked 'a' or 'an' and say the noun aloud with the article.

Let us learn — C (p.31): students work through all three sentences independently, writing each blank. Teacher then projects or writes answers, and students self-check, circling any blank they got wrong and correcting it.
Pair challenge: each pair writes two new sentences of their own using 'a' and 'an' correctly — one must include a word starting with a vowel. Pairs swap and check each other's articles.
Three pairs share their sentences with the class. Class gives a thumbs-up if both articles are correct, or corrects the error together by naming the starting sound of the noun.

periods.teacher_notes: Part C sentences contain multiple blanks in a single sentence — for instance, 'a brown hen laid an egg' — so students must apply the rule twice consecutively; this is where errors cluster. The fruit sentence ('an apricot, a chikoo, and an orange') is particularly useful because students may know apricot and orange as vowel starters but may guess at chikoo — draw attention to the /ch/ consonant sound explicitly.
materials: 'A' / 'An' response cards (two small cards per student, or fingers on lap for silent signalling)

periods.activity_title: Writing About My Friend: Guided Sentence Completion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.32): complete the 'My Friend' paragraph by filling in personal details about a real friend.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the six sentence frames on the board and reads them aloud with a sample friend in mind — filling blanks with made-up details ('My friend's name is Priya. She is a girl.…'). Students watch and listen to understand the task before writing.

Students spend a quiet moment thinking about which friend they will write about and mentally completing each sentence before picking up a pencil. Teacher reminds them that every detail should be true.

Let us write — B (p.32): students fill in all six blanks independently in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, checking that pronouns match ('He/She') and that the last line 'I love my friend' is included.
Peer-share: students read their completed paragraph to a partner. The partner checks that every blank is filled and that pronouns are consistent. Partners offer one positive comment.
Two or three volunteers read their paragraph aloud to the class. Teacher gives brief oral feedback on one strength — e.g. correct pronoun use or a vivid detail about the friend's ambition.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence frame 'He/She wants to become ___' often produces generic answers like 'doctor'; prompt students to think of what they have actually heard their friend say about the future. The pronoun choice 'He/She' requires students to decide early — remind them to re-read the second blank after choosing the pronoun so 'His/Her' matches.
materials: Chalkboard or whiteboard (for displaying the six sentence frames)

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.33): draw Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle as characters from the story.

time_bands.activity: Teacher names each shape-friend from the story and asks a student to describe one property aloud — 'Circle is round with no sharp edges.' This verbal recall primes the hand before drawing begins.

Let us do — A (p.33): students draw all four shape-characters in the space provided, giving each shape a face or expression to show its 'personality' from the story. Teacher circulates, checking that each shape is geometrically accurate and recognisable.

Gallery walk: students place their books open on their desks and walk past three neighbours' drawings, silently noting which shape they find most expressive. Teacher prompts them to look at how the shape itself — round, four-equal-sided, triangular — comes through in the drawing.

Each student says one sentence about a classmate's drawing: 'I like how ___'s Circle looks happy because it has no sharp corners.' Class closes with the idea that each shape looks different but all four are friends.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle describe their own properties in the story, students should be able to draw each shape accurately — if a student draws a lopsided square, gently ask, 'Did the story say a square has four equal sides or different sides?' The goal of the activity is expressive character drawing, so a roughly correct geometric shape with a personality is better than a perfect shape with no character.
materials: Drawing space in the textbook or a blank sheet of paper

periods.activity_title: Creating a Shape Picture: Inspired by the Cityscape

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — A (p.33): draw an original picture using geometric shapes as building blocks, inspired by the cityscape illustration.

time_bands.activity: Teacher directs students to the cityscape illustration on p.33 and leads a picture-walk: 'What shapes do you see making the mountains? What shapes are the buildings? What is the sun?' Students name shapes as the teacher points.

Students plan their own picture on a small rough sketch — deciding which shapes they will use and what those shapes will represent (a house, a tree, an animal, a vehicle). Teacher asks two students to share their plan aloud.

Let us explore — A (p.33): students draw their shape-picture independently. Teacher circulates encouraging deliberate shape use — 'Can you add a rectangle somewhere? What could it be in your picture?'

Students share their picture with a neighbour and say two sentences: 'I used a ___ to make a ___ because ___.' The class ends with students seeing how the same four shapes can make entirely different pictures — echoing the star's message about every shape having its own value.

periods.teacher_notes: The cityscape on p.33 uses triangles for mountains and rooftops, rectangles for buildings, and circles for the sun — mention these specifically during the picture-walk so students have concrete starting points for their own composition. Resist the urge to model a full sample picture; a rough two-shape sketch on the board is enough to spark ideas without constraining creativity.
materials: Blank drawing paper or notebook page

periods.activity_title: Re-reading for Fluency and a Quick Friendly Caption

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — items 1–5 (p.29): re-read for fluency, focusing on the shapes' dialogue sections.
Let us write — B (p.32): write a one-sentence caption describing a friend using the story's theme of acceptance.

time_bands.activity: Repeated reading: each student reads pp.25–29 aloud at their own pace while the teacher circulates and listens in. Every two minutes the teacher signals one student to read the current page aloud for the class. Focus is on smooth reading, not comprehension questions.

Whole-class review of the Let us think items 1–5 (p.29): teacher reads each question aloud, students give the answer from memory without opening books, then confirm by locating the relevant line. This builds the habit of returning to the text.

Picture-prompted writing: students draw a small thumbnail of themselves and their friend side by side, then write one sentence beneath it using the frame 'My friend ___ and I are different, but together we ___.' Teacher models one example on the board first.
Three students share their caption sentence. The class listens for whether the sentence captures both difference and friendship, echoing the star's lesson. Teacher gives brief positive oral feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: Pairing fluency work with the comprehension questions from the story lets students discover that smooth reading helps them recall details accurately — a connection worth naming briefly. For the caption, watch for students who write 'My friend and I are good' without naming a difference; prompt them to think of one way they and their friend are unlike, just as Circle and Square were unlike.

periods.activity_title: Every Shape Has a Place: Whole-Chapter Celebration

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents four objects: a biscuit (rectangle), a ladoo tin lid (circle), a samosa wrapper (triangle), and a chocolate (rectangle/square). Students identify each shape and recall what the matching character in the story boasted about it. This grounds the synthesis in the story's own language.

Retelling relay: the class retells the story together, one sentence at a time around the room. The teacher starts — 'Four shape-friends started arguing' — and each student continues, keeping the plot order: boasting, the star's arrival, and the final lesson of friendship.

Word-work spotlight: teacher holds up a card with a noun ('orange', 'book', 'umbrella', 'square') and students call out 'a' or 'an' and form a sentence using that noun — drawing on the article rule explored across the chapter.

Independent writing: each student writes three sentences beginning with 'My favourite shape is ___ because ___. In the story, ___ said ___. In real life, I can see ___ in ___.' Teacher circulates and gives brief written ticks or a single correction note.

Observational gallery: students walk to the window or look around the room for thirty seconds, then return to their seats and tell a partner one sentence naming a shape they spotted and one real-world object it forms — closing the chapter with the star's invitation to look around and notice how every shape has its own value.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together every strand of the chapter — the four shapes' properties from the story, the article rule from the word-work, the friendship theme from writing, and the shapes-in-the-world observation from the beyond-text activities. The retelling relay is deliberately unscripted so students connect story knowledge rather than recite; if the relay stalls, prompt with a shape name rather than a line from the text.
materials: Real or pictured objects: biscuit, round lid, samosa, chocolate
Noun flashcards for word-work (orange, book, umbrella, square)

items.source_lo: Student identifies key events and evaluates character claims using a prose story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four shape-friends argue about superiority; the wise star resolves their dispute by affirming each shape's unique value.
items.item_stem: Read the statements below and write True or False next to each one.

options.text: Circle boasted that it had no sharp edges and was beautiful.
Square claimed that its four sides are all different in length.
The four shape-friends asked a star to help them settle their argument.
The star decided that Rectangle was the most beautiful shape of all.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True (Circle says it is round and beautiful with no sharp edges). 2 — False (Square boasts that all four of its sides are equal). 3 — True (the shapes agree to ask the first person they meet, who turns out to be a star). 4 — False (the star says all shapes are friends and each has its own value; she names no winner).

items.source_context: Four shape-friends argue about superiority; the wise star resolves their dispute by affirming each shape's unique value.
items.item_stem: In the story, Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle all argued about who was the best. Do you think any one of them was really the best? Write two or three sentences explaining what the star taught them and whether you agree with her.

expected_elements: States the star's lesson: all shapes have value.
Refers to at least one shape's specific boast.
Gives a personal view with a reason.

items.item_stem: Listen carefully. Your teacher will describe what one of the shape-friends — Circle, Square, Triangle, or Rectangle — said about itself in the story. Choose the correct shape from the four options below.

what_each_option_reveals.A: A student choosing Circle may remember Circle's boast about no sharp edges and confuse 'equal sides' with 'no sides'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: A student choosing Triangle may know Triangle has three sides but not recall that Square specifically claimed four equal sides.
what_each_option_reveals.B: A student choosing Rectangle may recall the two long and two short sides description but has not noticed that those sides are not all equal.

teacher_guide.note: Teacher reads aloud: 'This shape said it has four sides and all four sides are the same length. It also said you can find it in sweets.' Correct answer is Square.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are the star in the story. In two or three sentences, tell the four shape-friends what you would say to stop their argument. Use the star's idea that every shape is special in its own way.

expected_elements: Addresses the shapes as friends, not rivals.
Mentions that each shape has its own unique quality.
Encourages them to work together or stop fighting.
